sections.context: The app's functions work (pen, text, box, arrow, lasso, eraser, pages, panes, sling prompt were hand-tested on 2026-11-11) but the window says nothing about its state. A tool change (cmd+4, cmd+5) gives zero feedback: no indicator, no cursor change. Nothing lists the 41 commands or their keys. The lasso selection is a thin grey rectangle without handles, the sidebar is one bare word, items at the canvas origin sit flush against the pane border, the focus border dominates a single pane, and the window is a fixed 960x600. This follows SPEC P6 ("No chrome") read literally, and O4 (key commands not decided). The owner decided: keep the no-chrome look but make every state visible (active tool and colour in a pane footer, a cursor per tool, a brief flash when a command runs, clear selection handles and text caret); discovery through a key overlay, a command palette and the macOS menu bar; P6 is reworded, not dropped. Six mockups (pen idle, tool change, selection and sling, key overlay, command palette, menu bar) on the owner's design board are the visual reference; the owner's markup on them amends the steps below.
sections.approach: One source of truth, three views. Extend the pure `commands` module into a registry: each Command gets a title and a group, and the Keymap answers command -> chord from the live config, with one function that prints a chord in macOS glyphs. The key overlay, the command palette, the menu bar, the footer's key hint and the tool flash all read that registry, so a rebind in config.toml shows everywhere and a new command appears in all of them with no extra code. All decisions stay in pure modules under `crates/app/src/scene` (new: status line, flash, overlay, palette; changed: select, shapes, sling, sidebar) and return Labels/Borders the existing Scene already carries; `platform` only gains a cursor setter, an NSMenu builder and a resize event. No daemon, control or core change: this is app-only, so no new verb. Two new commands (`show-keys` cmd+/, `show-commands` cmd+k) go through Command::ALL, config.example.toml and its completeness test. Each step ships its own tests in the pure module, a CHANGELOG line, and the ARCHITECTURE/SPEC edit when a contract changes. The palette lists registry commands only; the mockup's "Open workspace…" row and "4 of 38" count are placeholders, not scope.

sections.context: Slings reach an agent only through a 'claude --print' process slingerd spawns under tight limits (fixed tools, dontAsk, no user config, no MCP). The owner wants the agent to behave like a normal Claude Code session. SPEC section 5 already says a plain Claude Code session joins the list when it starts to listen. Owner feedback 2026-11-12: ship a /tldraw-listen equivalent.
sections.approach: A second delivery kind, listen. 'session_listen {workspace, wait}' is a long poll (the canvas_changes pattern, wait capped at MAX_WAIT_MS): it returns the next sling queued for the workspace's agent, or none. A sling with no profile goes to the agent's queue when a listener is attached (waiting, seen in the last seconds, or working on a sling it took) or when no process runs; otherwise to the process as today. A sling that names a profile goes only to a process, as today. The queued sling is the same message as text: the packet's images are written to the packet directory (the canvas_read pattern, at=<dir> in the header), line 1 names the agent, and the note tells a listener to pass --agent and set its status. Taking a sling sets the agent working. A reply that cannot be written puts the sling back. The pure state (queue, attached, the message text) lives in the core; the daemon holds it behind a mutex and condvar; the CLI loops the poll until a sling comes, prints it and exits, so a background shell wakes the session. The plugin gets a /slinger-listen command. The app shows a queued sling with nobody listening.

sections.context: The owner wants to read and mark up PDFs with the pen, cut sections out of them onto thinking canvases, and sling marked-up pages to an agent that sees both the ink and the page under it. Slinger has no PDF or image support today: SPEC section 4 and docs/design/canvas-file.md list images as not in v1, so this starts with a spec change.
sections.approach: A PDF is not a new pane or document type. It is one new canvas item kind `pdf` (frame, hash: the PDF's blob id, page, optional crop in PDF points). An opened PDF is a canvas of these items stacked top to bottom on one canvas page, with ordinary ink over it, so pen, lasso, undo, pages, sling and packets work unchanged. A snippet is the same item with a crop, copied through the existing clipboard path onto any canvas: vector-sharp, linked to its source, no pixel blobs. The PDF's bytes go into the record as a blob. The core treats the PDF as opaque and never parses it. Only the macOS app can draw a PDF (PDFKit / CoreGraphics; slingerd also ships for Linux), so the app draws pages in platform/pdf.rs and, at sling time, renders the PDF under the slung ink and extracts the words in those regions; the packet carries crops of the ink over the page plus a line of the exact words per cluster. The core's render draws ink over a supplied backdrop, which needs a small PNG decoder (miniz_oxide is already a dependency). A canvas made from a PDF opens in reader mode: locked vertical scroll and fit to the pane's width, nothing else. Open design point for the note (B6): clustering happens in the daemon, so the app does not know which regions a sling needs. Lean: the app sends each PDF page the selection touches at packet scale and the daemon crops (one request). Alternative: the app asks the daemon for the regions first, then renders only those (fewer pixels, a new verb).

risks: The core must never parse a PDF: page count and sizes come from the app (PDFKit). A canvas put of a PDF from the CLI alone has no source for them and is out of the first cut.
A sling sent from the CLI alone carries no PDF pixels or words, because only the app can render. The packet must still be valid (the item line names the blob and page).
Backdrops grow the sling: whole pages at packet scale may cost many image tokens. Measure tokens per sling as Spike B did before picking between whole pages and two steps.
A PNG decoder in the core must take what AppKit writes (all five filters, the colour types it emits), or the app must write a form the core fixes. Decide in the design note.
A scanned PDF has no text: the words line is absent and the pixels carry it alone.
A PDF blob lives in one machine's record: a canvas opened on a second machine lacks it until the record is copied (O8, D15).
Old readers keep an unknown item kind verbatim (canvas-file.md, Versions), but the app before this change must not crash on a `pdf` item: check the mirror skips it.
Reader mode is scene and layout logic, not platform: keep the decision (is this canvas a PDF's) out of platform/.
Large PDFs: drawing hundreds of vector pages must stay smooth while the pen draws (P7). Draw only visible pages and cache.
File budgets (500 lines) and the layer rules: platform/pdf.rs holds the only new unsafe and PDFKit code; new objc2 features go in the root Cargo.toml.
acceptance: Opening a PDF in the app makes a canvas whose pages lie stacked on one canvas page, drawn sharp at any zoom, and the pane scrolls it vertically at the pane's width.
Pen ink, lasso, eraser and undo work over a PDF as on any canvas, and the eraser never removes a `pdf` item.
A box dragged on a PDF copies as a cropped `pdf` item that pastes onto another canvas and still draws after the app restarts.

A sling of ink circling text in a PDF gives the agent a crop that shows the ink over the page and a packet line with the exact words under it; an agent answers a question about the circled text correctly in scripts/e2e-sling.sh or a hand run.
A canvas file with `pdf` items round-trips through the codec, and a reader from before the kind keeps the items verbatim.
The core has no PDF parsing and no new forbidden token: cargo xtask check-all passes.
SPEC, docs/design/pdf.md, canvas-file.md, packet.md, service.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, the guide and the CHANGELOG describe the feature.
